positions/catholic-sacramental-validity/: Catholic (Augustinian) sacramental validity
Ex opere operato
Anti-Donatist view
Mixed-church ecclesiology

Sacraments rightly administered with the Church’s intention are valid regardless of the personal holiness of the minister, because Christ himself is their true minister; the visible Church is a mixed body until the last judgement.
Christ is the principal minister of every sacrament; the human minister is an instrument.
Baptism and ordination administered even by heretics or schismatics in the right form are valid (though not fruitful outside the Church) and are not repeated.
The Church on earth contains both wheat and tares (corpus permixtum), and purity is an eschatological, not present, condition.
Unity and charity are the marks of the true Church; schism destroys love.
John 1:33 ("the same is he which baptizeth with the Holy Ghost")
Philippians 1:15–18
Augustine, On Baptism, against the Donatists; Tractates on John 6

Rome under Pope Stephen (c.256) refused to rebaptise heretics, against Cyprian. The Council of Arles (314) ruled against rebaptising those baptised in the Trinitarian name. Optatus of Milevis (c.367) and above all Augustine (On Baptism, 400–401) formulated the theology, vindicated at the Conference of Carthage (411). Scholastics coined "ex opere operato", defined by Trent (Session 7, canon 8, 1547). Magisterial Protestants largely accepted the anti-Donatist principle (Augsburg Confession VIII; Thirty-Nine Articles XXVI).

It grounds the believer’s assurance in Christ’s action, not in the unverifiable holiness of a minister.
It matches Jesus’ teaching that the Church will be mixed until the end and Paul’s rejoicing that Christ is preached even from bad motives (Phil 1:18).
It preserves unity: schism in the name of purity sins against love, the greatest gift.
Donatists and later perfectionist movements argue that it tolerates corruption and severs sacrament from holiness of life.
Orthodox theology traditionally treats sacraments outside the Church more strictly (debates over "economy" and reception of converts by baptism or chrismation).
Its association with imperial coercion against Donatists (approved by Augustine) set a dangerous precedent.
Augustine replied that a valid sacrament is not therefore fruitful: unrepentant ministers and recipients incur judgement, so holiness still matters.
Modern Catholic and Protestant theologians accept the validity principle while repudiating coercion, as Vatican II’s Dignitatis Humanae (1965) did.
Became the Western consensus on sacramental validity and the non-repetition of baptism and ordination.
Underlies modern ecumenical mutual recognition of baptism (e.g. BEM, 1982).
Shaped debates over the validity of orders (Anglican, Old Catholic) and over abusive clergy.
positions/supersessionism/oneLine: In Christ the promises to Israel reach their goal, and the Church of Jews and Gentiles is now the one people of God, so that ethnic Israel no longer has a distinct covenant standing apart from Christ.
positions/supersessionism/coreClaims/0: Jesus is Israel’s Messiah, the true Israel and the seed of Abraham (Gal 3:16, 29).
positions/supersessionism/coreClaims/1: Gentile believers are grafted into the one olive tree; there is one people of God, not two (Eph 2:11–22).
positions/supersessionism/coreClaims/2: The Mosaic covenant was provisional and is now "old" and "ready to vanish away" (Heb 8:13).
positions/supersessionism/coreClaims/3: Jews are saved, like Gentiles, through faith in Christ; many fulfilment theologians expect a future large-scale turning of Jews to Christ (Rom 11:26).
positions/supersessionism/coreClaims/4: Most modern advocates distinguish "fulfilment" from punitive replacement and repudiate antisemitism.
positions/supersessionism/origin: Implicit in debates of the 2nd century (Epistle of Barnabas, Justin’s Dialogue c.155, Melito’s Peri Pascha c.170) and in Augustine’s witness doctrine; it was the near-universal patristic, medieval and Reformation view, and remains the default framework of Orthodox, much Catholic and covenant-theology Protestant thought, though its "punitive" forms have been widely repudiated since 1945.
positions/supersessionism/strongestArgum: The New Testament repeatedly applies Israel’s titles ("a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation") to the mixed Jewish–Gentile church (1 Pet 2:9).
Paul insists that "they are not all Israel, which are of Israel" and that Abraham’s true children are those of faith (Rom 9:6; Gal 3:7).
Hebrews explicitly calls the Sinai covenant obsolete; a continuing separate covenant would make Christ unnecessary for Jews, contradicting Acts 4:12.
It preserves the unity of the people of God across both testaments rather than dividing God’s purposes in two.
positions/supersessionism/strongestObjec: Romans 11:28–29 says Jews who reject the gospel remain "beloved for the fathers’ sakes" because God’s gifts and calling are irrevocable (Soulen, Kinzer).
Historically it fed the "teaching of contempt" and contributed to persecution culminating in a culture that made the Shoah possible.
Dispensationalists argue it spiritualises concrete promises about land and nation that God swore unconditionally (Gen 15; Jer 31:35–37).
positions/supersessionism/responses/0: Fulfilment theologians reply that Israel’s election is fulfilled, not cancelled, in the Jewish Messiah, and that Romans 11 anticipates Jewish faith in Christ rather than a separate path.
positions/supersessionism/responses/1: They accept the historical indictment of punitive anti-Judaism but argue it was a betrayal of Paul’s warning against Gentile arrogance (Rom 11:18–20), not a necessary consequence of the doctrine.
positions/supersessionism/responses/2: On land promises they point to Hebrews 11:10–16 and Romans 4:13 (Abraham "heir of the world"), reading the land as a type of the renewed creation.
positions/supersessionism/consequences/0: Shaped the Church’s self-understanding as the "new Israel" and its reading of the Old Testament as Christian Scripture.
positions/supersessionism/consequences/1: Provided the theological background for medieval anti-Jewish polemic and legislation.
positions/supersessionism/consequences/2: Since Nostra Aetate (1965) many churches have revised or nuanced it; the debate now centres on "post-supersessionist" alternatives.
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/oneLine: God’s covenant with the Jewish people remains irrevocable and valid; Christians must reject every form of replacement theology, whether by holding that Jews are saved within their own covenant or by confessing a church of two distinct but united communities.
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/coreCla: "The gifts and calling of God are without repentance" (Rom 11:29): Israel’s election endures.
Strong form: Jews relate to God through the Sinai covenant, Gentiles through Christ (two covenants or "two ways").

Moderate (bilateral) form: Jesus is Israel’s Messiah, but the Jewish people’s covenant identity and Torah observance remain God-willed, and the church should be a communion of Jewish and Gentile ekklesiai.
Christian theology must be reconstructed after the Shoah to remove structural supersessionism (Soulen).
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/origin: Anticipated by the Jewish philosopher Franz Rosenzweig (Star of Redemption, 1921) and the Anglican James Parkes (1930s); developed after the Holocaust by Paul van Buren, Lloyd Gaston (Paul and the Torah, 1987), John Gager and Krister Stendahl; reframed as "post-supersessionism" by R. Kendall Soulen (1996) and Mark Kinzer (Postmissionary Messianic Judaism, 2005).
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/stronge: Paul nowhere says God has revoked Israel’s covenant; he says the opposite (Rom 11:1, 29).
In Acts, Jewish believers including Paul remain Torah-observant (Acts 21:20–26), implying a continuing Jewish vocation.
Theology that once legitimated contempt must be tested by its fruits; repentance after Auschwitz requires more than condemning violence.
It honours Judaism’s self-understanding as a living covenant faith rather than a superseded relic.
Strong two-covenant views seem to contradict "no man cometh unto the Father, but by me" (John 14:6) and the apostles’ preaching to Jews first (Acts 2–4; Rom 1:16).
Paul’s own anguish for unbelieving Israel (Rom 9:1–3; 10:1) makes little sense if Jews are already saved apart from Christ.
Critics (e.g. many evangelicals and Messianic Jews) argue that refusing to share the gospel with Jews is a new kind of exclusion.
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/respons: Bilateral theologians (Kinzer, Soulen) do not deny Christ’s universal mediation; they deny only that Jewish faithfulness to Torah is abolished, and see Israel’s "no" as mysteriously within God’s plan (Rom 11:25–32).
Two-covenant theologians read Romans 11:26 ("all Israel shall be saved") as God’s own sovereign act, not as a mission mandate, and note that Paul describes himself as apostle to the Gentiles.
positions/two-covenant-bilateral/consequ: Underlies Christian–Jewish dialogue statements and the renunciation of organised missions to Jews by several churches.
Rekindled scholarship on Paul as a Jewish thinker (the "Paul within Judaism" school).
Strongly contested by evangelical and Messianic Jewish missions such as Jews for Jesus.
positions/messianic-jewish/oneLine: Jews who believe Jesus (Yeshua) is Israel’s Messiah should remain Jews, keeping Sabbath, festivals and Jewish identity, in congregations that bear witness to Israel’s Messiah.
positions/messianic-jewish/coreClaims/0: Yeshua is the promised Messiah of Israel and the divine saviour of all.
positions/messianic-jewish/coreClaims/1: Jewish identity and covenant practices are not abolished for Jewish believers (Acts 21:20–26; 1 Cor 7:18).
positions/messianic-jewish/coreClaims/2: Messianic congregations are a remnant of Israel within the wider body of Messiah.
positions/messianic-jewish/coreClaims/3: Most Messianic Jews affirm a future for national Israel and many support the modern State of Israel.
positions/messianic-jewish/origin: Jewish followers of Jesus formed the earliest church; distinct Jewish-Christian groups (Nazarenes, Ebionites) faded by the 5th century. Modern Hebrew Christianity grew in the 19th century (Joseph Rabinowitz’s Kishinev congregation, 1884; Hebrew Christian Alliance of America, 1915) and became the Messianic Jewish movement after 1967 (Jews for Jesus, 1973; MJAA, 1975).
positions/messianic-jewish/strongestArgu: The first church was entirely Jewish and Torah-observant (Acts 2–21); Gentile inclusion did not require Jews to stop being Jews.
Paul circumcised Timothy and offered sacrifices in the Temple (Acts 16:3; 21:26), modelling Jewish faithfulness in Messiah.
It removes the historical demand that Jewish converts renounce their people, which made conversion feel like betrayal.
positions/messianic-jewish/strongestObje: Jewish communities regard it as deceptive missionary Christianity under Jewish dress; Israel’s Supreme Court (1989) denied Messianic Jews automatic citizenship as Jews under the Law of Return.
Some Christians fear it reintroduces a two-tier church or the "Judaizing" rejected in Galatians.
Post-supersessionist critics question its frequent alliance with evangelism aimed specifically at Jews.
positions/messianic-jewish/responses/0: Messianic leaders reply that Galatians forbids imposing Torah on Gentiles as a condition of salvation, not Jewish practice of Torah by Jews.
positions/messianic-jewish/responses/1: They argue that Jewish identity is a matter of descent and covenant, which faith in Israel’s Messiah fulfils rather than cancels.
positions/messianic-jewish/consequences/: Several hundred thousand Messianic believers worldwide, concentrated in the USA and Israel.
Revived the question of Jewish practice within the church and fed "bilateral ecclesiology".
A persistent flashpoint in Jewish–Christian relations.
